#3463. ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’

Jack O’Connell was feeling a little bashful. Seated outside for coffee, taking in the fresh fall air at the remote Salamander Resort in Middleburg, Virginia, the actor revealed that communication between him and Oscar-winning filmmaker Danny Boyle began long before he was cast as the lead in the director’s latest film, “Ink.”

“I used to write to Danny a lot. I wrote all the directors that I admire,” said the 36-year-old star from Derbyshire, England. “Not cap in hand, trying to get anything out of them, just letters of appreciation, lovely stuff that’s affected me and inspired me. ‘I hope we get to do it someday.’ And, in Danny’s case, we did.” Related Stories How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

Technically “Ink,” in which O’Connell plays influential newspaper editor Larry Lamb after he’s recruited by outcast media magnate Rupert Murdoch to take over The Sun tabloid in 1969, is the second time the actor has worked with Boyle. The pair first officially met when he was brought in to play antagonist Jimmy Crystal in last year’s “28 Years Later,” directed by Boyle, and more prominently in January’s “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” directed by Nia DaCosta.

“It was right before I went and shot ‘Sinners,’” he said, referencing another major turn as a villain that loomed prominently over cinema this year. “The initial meeting wasn’t an audition. I just didn’t have the role. It was a meeting discussing the role with Danny and Nia.” It was the first time Boyle had acknowledged O’Connell, though he had a sneaking suspicion that he had been on the director’s radar for a while, having starred on the same iconic British teen drama “Skins” from which Boyle had found the star of his Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire.”

“Listen, he cast Dev [Patel]. He knew about ‘Skins.’ I think his daughter put him onto ‘Skins’ in the first place. So whether or not he stuck it out for our generation, I don’t know,” said O’Connell.

It’s been almost two decades since he first played fan favorite Cook as part of the second generation of the trailblazing E4 series, which ran from 2007 to 2013. “Skins” still stands out as an experience that helped shape his ethos as an actor. “I certainly felt like we were on the coolest show around. It was so amazingly written. The directors we had were brilliant. The whole model of the way that you audition en masse and then they find their characters. I love that,” said O’Connell. “It’s really quite pure, isn’t it? People are just getting the roles because of ability.”

The “Ink” star first trained as an actor at a free program in Nottingham called the Television Workshop, which eventually helped lead to his first breakout film role in the coming-of-age drama “This Is England.” However, it was “Skins” that felt like a “crash course” continuing education. “You’re doing all the heavy stuff, the tough stuff, the really laborious side of doing a TV show like that. But also the fun and the joy that gets provoked by all the art, the amazing writing and everything else,” said O’Connell. He’s quick to remind that notable “Skins” alumni include not just Patel, but also writers like Emmy winner Jack Thorne and Tony-nominated playwright Lucy Kirkwood.

But free programs like the Television Workshop are increasingly hard to come by, meaning there are less and less egalitarian-type opportunities in the United Kingdom for an actor from a working-class background like O’Connell’s to find their own “Skins.” Asked what he would tell the next generation of artists, the “Ink” star said, “I wouldn’t know what advice I would give nowadays, which is a shocking indictment.”

What attracted O’Connell to playing Lamb in “Ink,” a role that has brought him to the Middleburg Film Festival to receive the Spotlight Actor Award, was the opportunity to address how the UK, and the world in general, reached this place of inequality. “We see this man just excavate his morals, and his soul, and his decisions, and this newspaper. Being the best-selling newspaper, he’s had to part with what makes people more human. To me, it’s a comment on capitalism,” said the star. “The beginning of hyper capitalism, post-war England, and individual opportunity versus looking after everyone else and your responsibility within society. That was all just getting ripped up.”

“Ink” is an adaptation of James Graham’s 2017 play of the same name, with Graham also serving as the screenwriter of Boyle’s film. Another major factor in O’Connell’s decision to play Larry Lamb was working with the playwright and the director, who had come from a similar background. With Boyle, “I came to his work as a fan first, before I knew I was going to try and be an actor,” he said. “I remember watching ‘The Beach,’ and that made me want to go and see the world. And watching ‘Trainspotting’ and that made me want to never take heroin. But also the amazing soundtrack that’s in there and the fucking unforgettable performances.”

With “Ink” they were preparing to tell what O’Connell sees as a quintessentially British story, and “what [Danny’s] films have meant for British cinema and British culture as a result is undeniable. Thank fuck for Danny Boyle. He is an artist by every stretch of the word. I would argue that his films have perhaps meant the most to us as a collective growing up. His work at the Olympics opening ceremony makes you tingle to watch it. It is fucking monumental.”

Boyle is why O’Connell, an outsider to the film and TV industry in the same way Lamb was to the publishing industry, could still envision himself becoming an actor one day. “His style has been able to make you feel part of the film. It takes you along. You feel like you’re in the movie somehow. You don’t feel like an observer, like a spectator. They give you a feeling and mood as well,” he said.

As for Graham, “We’re not too far from each other in a particular pocket of the UK. And although my town and his town famously don’t get on — that’s all to do with football and Brian Clough and whatever else — but he is a dramatist. He’s also interested in analyzing culture and the culture around him and examining it,” said O’Connell. “He’s a great spokesman for under-representation in the industry at home because eight percent of the entire industry are from our background.”

The actor added, “Once he knew that I was somebody that could be trusted with his words, not someone who was going to try and fucking destroy them, we really hit it off.”

Here the three were, as what some would call a band of outsiders, telling a story about these insurgents to the distinguished Fleet Street, where the most esteemed newspapers like The Daily Mirror were published. Playing Lamb was a bit of an exercise in what would happen if O’Connell’s comeuppance led him toward the dark side. “The intoxication of power is something that really interests me. And Larry, he began as a socialist, voted Labour, celebrated socialist politicians. He left Fleet Street having been knighted by Margaret Thatcher. … Talk about excavation, a whole U-turn politics there, colluded with Rupert Murdoch in tearing up the unions and workers’ rights. Sold his soul,” said O’Connell.

“There’s a great contradiction with Larry that he begins as an outsider. Even within the duration of our film, he’s trying to become an insider. He wants to be part of that gang. In fact, that’s where he ended up, Sir Larry. So there’s a great contradiction in the man. So I can’t afford to go all the way ‘outsider with a chip on his shoulder,’” said the actor.

With “Ink” following the successes of “Sinners” and “28 Years Later” so quickly, O’Connell has a newfound feeling of security and sense of becoming that sought-after leading man. “It probably is my most mature role to date,” he said. “I look back on my career and I just feel so fortunate. There’s not a single regret. So if this is a new era, yeah, brilliant, bring it on. A lot of my heroes, a lot of their work that I really celebrate, were around my age, so maybe that is inspiring and gives me cause to kick on.”

Netflix will release “Ink” in select theaters across the United States on Friday, December 11. The film will debut on the streaming service on January 8, 2027.

#3462. You Can Get Microsoft Visual Studio Pro 2026 on Sale for Just $30 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3461. Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

Talent labs and mentorship programs are plentiful for aspiring filmmakers — but where do you turn when your career has already started, after your first movie or on the precipice of one, and especially when filmmaking can be such a lonely enterprise?

Enter Square Peg Social, the Austin, Texas-based filmmaking summit launched by Lars and Amy Knudsen and Ari Aster that offers four days of singular community-building: brutally honest advice, commiseration, and idea exchange shared among 35 participants, with the program now in its second year.

A weekend of panels, discussion, and camaraderie designed for filmmakers at the early stages of their career, this year’s talent-incubating event was even crashed by the likes of Zach Cregger and Richard Linklater — both of whom were down to get frank about their filmmaking highs and lows. (In fall 2025, IndieWire did a deep dive into Square Peg Social’s first year, just to show how much the event has already grown.) Related Stories ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’ How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

But the program’s stable of 2026 mentors and panelists — i.e., filmmakers keen not only to open up to new filmmakers about their own struggles, but also to scout new talent — also counted “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything” director Lance Oppenheim, “Sing Sing” filmmaker Greg Kwedar, “The First Omen” director Arkasha Stevenson, and “Mother Mary” director David Lowery among them.

The closed-door, off-the-record, noncompetitive summit opened to applicants in May, later unfolding from September 17-21. Partners including the Austin Film Society, Belvedere, and Airbnb offset the cost, besides a modest application fee, for participants to hole up for four days and nights at Soho House that don’t promise job opportunities — but instead, the kind of lasting industry connections that can take years (and many starts and stops) to build. Also, no job opportunities isn’t entirely true. Take last year’s Square Peg Social mentee Yona Strauss, who’s now working for Knudsen and Aster’s Square Peg.

Just a sampling of this year’s participating producers and directors: producer Annie Huang, who worked on franchise IP like “Barbie” and “Wicked” at major studios; Jack Auen, co-founder of the filmmaking collective Cosmic Salon, which this year directed the New York critics’ favorite “Chronovisor”; Emmy-winning director of the Netflix short “The Turnaround,” Kyle Thrash; SXSW 2026 Neon Auteur Award winner Oliver Woolf; and many more who have their foot in the door, but are ready to cross the threshold.

IndieWire spoke to Lars Knudsen and Aster (who also co-founded the production company Square Peg, which this year backed “The Drama” and “Primetime”), plus Stevenson, Oppenheim, and Kwedar, along with three participants, to replay the on-the-ground experience in Austin. Late nights, early mornings, and vulnerabilities abounded across a long (but in some ways too short) weekend of intimate panels, small group sessions, and candid remarks from established filmmakers about the times they were trying to hold their own projects together with Scotch tape and paper clips. Think of it like a mini summer camp devoted to obsessive ambition.

“When you’ve been doing it for this long, sometimes it feels like you’re just a little bit going through the motions. You’re going from movie to movie to movie, and you sometimes forget why we do this thing that we do. We’re in this world working with these artists where they don’t have a plan B. Having now worked with 30, 40 filmmakers, I realized that when my wife brought up the idea of doing something because she has her own aversions to the industry, and that there isn’t really — it sounds cliché — but there just isn’t a lot of kindness or compassion or openness in our industry.

“There’s a lot of fear, there’s a lot of rejection. We wanted to create a space for filmmakers where there’s radical transparency and where it was truly, truly focused on a selfless thing: helping young filmmakers navigate the industry at a time in their career where things can either take off or not, and really demystifying the process of making movies, especially during the stage where they’re often in the back seat, which is financing or casting. Because for all these filmmakers that I work with and all the filmmakers that we’ve invited there, even the producers, it’s the first thing to think about when they wake up and the last thing to think about when they go to bed. Nothing is more important. I wanted to create an event where that is treated with the utmost importance, almost like it’s a life-or-death thing because it is all they want to do.”

“When Lars and Amy first broached the idea with me, I realized that it was something that I wish I had when I got out of school [at AFI], because I really did have to navigate that on my own. I was making a lot of shorts with whatever money I could raise and writing screenplays and trying to get one screenplay going. When that failed, writing something else and really looking for any sort of mentorship or guidance, It’s a very demoralizing process, and it was very, very hard for me to find traction, and it hasn’t gotten easier. It’s as bad as it’s ever been. There’s just so much uncertainty right now in the industry, not just for filmmakers. Even the lives of these studios are suddenly in danger and in question.

“There are a lot of filmmakers that Lars and I have been championing and films that we’ve been trying to get financing for that have proven almost impossible… It felt like a good thing to create a space where filmmakers can come together and commiserate and share experiences and connect. More important than even the connections that are made between the mentors and the mentees here are actually the relationships made among the people who are attending. A lot of them end up working together because we have producers and directors coming in. Last year proved really successful, and I would just say it was refreshing for us, too, that it galvanized us to keep doing this. Because last year it was almost an experiment: Will this work? How will we feel having done this? … Everybody walked away feeling good and feeling like it was a really useful and positive experience.”

“I’ve never really had the opportunity to just hang out with so many great filmmakers, not only just working filmmakers whose work I’ve loved, like David Lowery, who I’ve idolized for so long, but there’s so many filmmakers that were actually in the program as participants whose work I also have really admired. So having a space where we could all just kind of talk and vent and really nerd out on stuff that you never really get the opportunity to do.

“Because this was so filmmaker-driven and filmmaker-led, it encouraged the spirit of vulnerability [where] everyone really went there. I felt like maybe I should go back to therapy or something, but I felt like this was a great opportunity to therapize and also dump all of my feelings into a forum where you could just be open and honest about the process of making films… Most people had made features before, and were in the process of making features. It felt much more like we were at a film festival and everyone was able to connect with each other in a much deeper way, more than anything I’ve been to before.

“The first night I was there, I stayed up till like three in the morning, and I went on one of those electric scooters, the limes with Lars and Christian [Vasquez], my producer, and a producer from the event, too. We went to Whataburger and just kept talking. I think that was sort of the vibe. I don’t know. I guess everyone was encouraged to hang out for as long as they wanted to and to kick back and relax. There was another night we closed down the Soho House lounge bar, and Amy was like, ‘Let’s keep hanging out.’ So we were outside the bar, and everybody pulled together all of the drinks in their mini bar, and we created an ad hoc bar outside of the Soho House, and we kept drinking and hanging.”

“I don’t think you can really do film if you have a plan B because there’s always an escape hatch, and film requires every single atom of your body, mind and soul. It naturally becomes a very therapeutic place. I think because we’re all in this constant state of obsession, that can get really tiring, and it can get really lonely. … [The industry] attracts very sensitive souls. [With Square Peg Social] I didn’t even realize how badly I needed it until the first year. I’d known Amy and Lars before that, and Amy said that she wanted to start a Social. … I thought it would be much smaller, smaller. It ended up being this great big thing where, yeah, it does feel like a therapy circle, really.

“Everyone was really struck by the safety of the event. There was this unspoken agreement that everybody would be checking your egos at the door, and that this would be a very safe place to share your personal vulnerabilities, which is exceptionally rare in film because resources are so limited, and it’s just naturally a very competitive industry. Letting yourself be very, very vulnerable in front of your peers is something you were, in a sense, trained not to do but sometimes desperately need. At Square Peg, also, the line between mentee and mentor blurs quite a bit, which is why I think it’s so beneficial for everybody who goes there.

“It kind of reminds me of summer camp a little bit because you’re up until two or three in the morning talking to people, and then you’re up at eight again.”

“I always think of this term, like, whenever you take an elevator up, if you get to the top floor, send it back down for someone else to get on. [Square Peg] is one of the busiest production companies working today. To dedicate this weekend for emerging artists to have a forum where they can come and feel completely comfortable being very vulnerable with their ambitions, but also the things that they’re afraid of, and to hear that echoed from industry mentors who are being just as vulnerable about their ambitions and the things that they struggle with and the heartbreaks they’ve had, it’s an amazing table that’s set.

“I had ulterior motives in the, in the sense that Clint [Bentley] and I have started this new company, Ethos, and we have a deal at Netflix to finance films from emerging artists, and so I was also there … to look for talent. We’ll be following up with a lot of these artists to just hear more about the films they want to make. One thing that I appreciated about it was that it wasn’t like a pitch fest. You’re not there to pitch your project. You’re there to soak it in and learn.

“It had this healthy blend of these panels, and not the normal kind of panel. One was a panel of filmmakers led off by Ari and Lars, telling a very, very brutally honest story of how hard one of their films was to make. That kind of created a pathway for how the rest of the weekend would unfold.”

“I think the whole reason anyone works in film is that we were once kids making videos in the woods with our friends, making with a shitty camera. And there’s nothing else in this world, and I think I probably speak for everyone, where I can’t imagine film is the only thing that’s our main passion and hobby and something we can also make a career out of. So there was never a plan B at all. Whenever someone asked me, ‘What do you think you’d do if you couldn’t do anything film-adjacent?’ I have literally no idea, maybe a teacher or something. That’s super nice that Lars and the rest of Square Peg was saying that there is no plan B. There’s only: If it takes longer to get to Plan A, then it takes longer to get to Plan A.

“I remember on the very first day before we even properly began, Lars did a little speech with Ari, and Lars was like, ‘We’re going to be 100 percent transparent with you guys.’ And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that’s cool, but I wonder how transparent.’ And by the end of it, I was like, ‘Fuck me, that was transparent.’ There really was nothing off the table.”

“It was definitely something that I’ve never experienced before in this industry, to experience that level of candor and to hear these traumatic experiences that they have gone through in not a sensationalistic way, but almost in a very personal and almost relatable way, despite me having never experienced that level of millions of dollars of movie budget making — but on a personal level of how the heartbreaks had felt for them individually and the hardships of filmmaking. Coming into this program, there are so many people within our cohort who are incredibly talented, who have accomplished so many things. And coming into it, oftentimes you’ll have a fear of: ‘OK, how do I compare in relation to their accomplishments?’ But in hearing Lars and Ari talk about their own hardships, I think that’s what influenced me to really share some of mine coming up in the industry and producing independently.

“Some of the traumatic experiences that I have also faced are ones that I feel like I have to not talk about or hide from people, for fear of them looking like mistakes or of me looking like I’m not good enough to be doing this. And we were able to share that, like Ollie [Woolf] and I, in our own little producer’s therapy session with the mentors, with Lars. That was really healing for me.”

“[Ari, Lars, and the mentors are] on, not a different level, but they’re all going through similar issues and this and that, whether it’s a low budget or a higher budget type of ordeal. Everyone’s going through the same thing in their own way, in a sense. Just to know the people that I’ve been looking up to for a very long time, the reason in large part why I got into making films, to know that they’re going through similar things and just keep going, and it’s fine. No matter what level we’re going to be at, there’s still something to navigate. So I thought it was very cool to see, over the course of five days, to hear these individual experiences and stuff and how you could relate it back to what we’re going through right now and where we are.

“It was information overload in the best way possible. At a certain point, I hope I’m retaining everything that was said over those five days because it was nonstop, all useful information. I wasn’t even taking notes at a certain point because I’m like, ‘I can’t write all this stuff down. I’m just going to try and soak it all in.'”

#3460. Avatar: The Last Airbender’s Zuko Prequel Is Only 3 Months Away, Here’s Who’s Returning

2026 has been an epic year for Avatar: The Last Airbender fans, with recent releases such as Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender and Avatar: Seven Havens. However, the year has also had its fair share of disappointments, most notably the cancellation of Avatar Studios' animated movie starring an adult Fire Lord Zuko. The project was reportedly in development before Paramount ultimately scrapped it in 2026. However, fans are now just three months away from the release of a Zuko-starring prequel, and he isn't returning alone.

We may not be getting the adult Zuko film that OG fans were frothing at the mouth for, but the world of Avatar: The Last Airbender will officially be taking fans back to Zuko's early days in exile with Avatar: The Last Airbender – Enter the Blue Spirit. This upcoming graphic novel from Dark Horse Comics will tell the story of Zuko adopting the Blue Spirit persona for the first time to save a remote Fire Nation colony.

After four years of waiting, fans of Netflix’s Blue Eye Samurai have plenty to look forward to in 2027, with two new releases coming to the franchise.

Brought to life by the creative talents of writer Faith Erin Hicks, artist Peter Wartman, and colorist Adele Matera, this 80-page story will be available for $13.99 on February 23, 2027. It will deliver a missing chapter from Zuko's story, set before Nickelodeon's original TV series. While the story will obviously see the return of the Fire Nation prince, we also have confirmation of two other characters who will appear, along with some speculation about who else we might see.

As a quick recap, Zuko first appears as the Blue Spirit in the original show during Season 1 of Avatar: The Last Airbender, specifically in Book One: Water, Episode 13, "The Blue Spirit." Zuko disguises himself as a masked swordsman to infiltrate Admiral Zhao's fortress and rescue Aang after his capture, giving himself another chance to receive credit for capturing the Avatar and, in turn, restoring his honor.

Now, AtLA is taking fans back in time with Enter the Blue Spirit, revisiting the early days of Zuko's exile and lifting the veil on the origins of his Blue Spirit persona. Below, readers can find the full synopsis for the upcoming graphic novel:

In the early months of Prince Zuko's exile, he and Iroh discover a long-forgotten Fire Nation colony along the coast of the Earth Kingdom. But when the Fire Nation demands larger quantities of the valuable ore the village produces for the war effort, the colonists' lives are suddenly at risk. Desperate to defend his people, even against his own homeland, Zuko becomes the Blue Spirit for the very first time. But if he's discovered thwarting the will of the Fire Lord, he'll lose any chance at regaining his honor and returning home.

Thanks to this synopsis, we have confirmation that fan-favorite Uncle Iroh will be returning in this prequel. This is both unsurprising and reassuring. AtLA fans know that Uncle Iroh was with Zuko from the very beginning of his banishment. The fact that Enter the Blue Spirit respects this piece of canon bodes well for the graphic novel staying true to the series' continuity and respecting the original source material, something longtime fans will undoubtedly expect from such a project.

Given that the premise of this prequel revolves around Zuko's banishment, and the fact that synopsis also makes direct reference to Fire Lord Ozai, we can all but guarantee that the Fire Lord will make an appearance as well, even if it's just through a flashback or in the opening pages of the graphic novel. While these are the only original series characters confirmed to return, we wouldn't be surprised if Azula also appears.

While she obviously wouldn't be accompanying Zuko on his exile, AtLA is no stranger to jumping between characters. We may even see flashbacks featuring Zuko's mother, Ursa, since this was common throughout the series whenever Zuko's story was explored. Other notable characters we might get a glimpse of include Mai and Ty Lee. Of course, this is all just speculation at this point, but we'd love to hear which side character you'd most like to see return in this next Avatar: The Last Airbender project.

Avatar: The Last Airbender – Enter the Blue Spirit TP from Dark Horse Comics will be available on February 23, 2027!

#3459. The 10 Greatest Soft Magic Systems in Books, Ranked

It was Brandon Sanderson, far and away one of the most prolific and downright legendary fantasy authors currently working, who coined the terms "hard magic system" and "soft magic system" back in 2007 with his essay Sanderson's First Law. Whereas hard magic systems have very clear rules and boundaries, making it abundantly clear to readers how they work, soft magic systems have far more vague and undefined limitations, prioritizing wonder and awe over strict mechanics.

When well-crafted, soft magic systems can be among the very best in the entire history of fantasy literature. Their nebulous, mysterious nature can imbue any given novel with an unparalleled sense of breathtaking mystique, upping the stakes and adding to the scale and scope of the story. From classics like The Lord of the Rings to modern masterpieces like The Poppy War, there are many incredible books with some incredible soft magic systems.

R. F. Kuang's debut novel was The Poppy War, the first installment in the trilogy of the same name and undeniable proof of Kuang's tremendous quality as a fantasy author. Inspired by the Second Sino-Japanese War, it's about an impoverished orphan who enters an elite military academy, only to discover that she has a lethal aptitude for shamanism right as a devastating war breaks out with a rival empire.

Saying that Kuang, who holds a degree in Chinese history from Georgetown University, put an awful lot of research into The Poppy War would be a massive understatement. But it's not just the historical realism that makes this one of the best grimdark books of all time, but also the engrossing magic system. Where many soft magic systems end up feeling like deus ex machina, Kuang manages to keep hers mysterious while still filling it with psychological, narrative, and thematic layers.

The Black Company series of dark fantasy novels is almost undeniably Glen Cook's magnum opus, composed of some of the most influential fantasy books of all time. The series follows an elite band of cynical mercenaries and sorcerers, chronicling their exploits over four decades from the perspective of their doctor-historian. The series definitely peaks with its first installment, The Black Company, but is worth reading in its entirety for those who love dark fantasy.

The whole saga was one of the first true modern grimdark fantasy book entries, and its soft magic system remains one of the most fascinating that the subgenre has ever delivered. Magic here is an ability so intrinsic to certain gifted individuals that there's no need for hard rules here. Since the series is narrated by a character who's not a wizard, it's naturally imbued with even more powerful ambiguity and uncertainty.

People who love cozy fantasy and are looking for a great new book to read without committing to an entire series ought to consider Sangu Mandanna's The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches. It's one of the most delightful cozy fantasy novels of the last six years, following a lonely witch who breaks the rules of her society by posting online magic videos. So, she's summoned to a remote English house to tutor three young orphan witches, finding romance and a new family.

It may not have the highest stakes or the most complex narrative, but that's what cozy fantasy is all about — it's also what makes this one of the best fantasy books of the 2020s so far. Its magic system is just as cozy as the story itself, with magic being a powerful force tied to witches' emotions and intuition. This angle helps the whole book feel all the more intimate, and makes it even easier to relate to the characters' feelings and mood.

Will George R. R. Martin ever actually deliver the conclusion of A Song of Ice and Fire? Fans have grown doubtful that he ever will, but even if The Winds of Winter never actually sees the light of day, this landmark saga would remain a must-read of the high fantasy genre. Starting with A Game of Thrones, the saga chronicles a brutal civil war between several noble houses for control of the Iron Throne, all while an ancient horror awakens beyond the edge of the world.

Virtually every exceptional installment of A Song of Ice and Fire is one of those books that belong on every fantasy lover's bucket list, and even though the series is not fundamentally about magic, it certainly contains plenty. Here, however, magic is an ancient, unknowable force operating well beyond the boundaries of human comprehension. Martin deliberately keeps things elusive and shrouded in mystery, which makes it feel dangerous, eerie, and distant.

Everyone loves a great fantasy drama that takes magic with full seriousness, but comedic fantasy is every bit as essential. And as far as comedic fantasy goes, it doesn't get much better than the work of Terry Pratchett. His Discworld series follows dozens of vastly different stories set on a flat planet balanced on the backs of four elephants who are themselves standing on the back of a giant turtle. Written by one of modern times' master satirists, it's a 41-novel series unlike any other.

From Night Watch to Small Gods to Guards! Guards!, Discworld is one of the fantasy book series with the best worldbuilding, which certainly includes a phenomenal magic system. Magic in Discworld is a brilliant subversion of the very idea of magic systems, used to interrogate human nature, characters' psyches, and the nature of fantasy storytelling itself. Though complex, it also provides the comedic fuel of many of the series' best outings.

Before one of the most perfect movies based on books, there was the book itself: Diana Wynne Jones' Howl's Moving Castle, the first installment in the Howl series. Highly influential and thoroughly delightful, this children's novel is the story of Sophie, who seeks refuge in a vain wizard's walking castle after a witch turns her into an old lady. There, she makes a pact with a fire demon to break both her curse and the wizard's.

Here, magic can be wielded simply by speaking life into inanimate objects, a system that operates on the same kind of soft rules that define the magic systems in oh so many of history's greatest classic folk tales. This approach makes it so that magic in Howl's Moving Castle is a response to the characters' emotions and thoughts, a simplicity which lets Jones embed that same magic in domestic activities with the utmost naturalism.

An orphaned boy discovers that he's a wizard on his eleventh birthday, going on to attend a magical boarding school and growing up to defeat the Dark Lord who murdered his parents. From such a seemingly simple, traditional Hero's Journey premise, the saga became the best-selling fiction book series of all time, all starting with the revolutionary Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (published in the United States as Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone).

Since these are all among the best-selling fantasy books of all time, this is also perhaps the most widely experienced soft magic system in the history of fantasy literature. Whimsical, intuitive, and often far more rooted in emotions than in particularly strict rules or limitations, Harry Potter's magic system sometimes flirts with elements that are on the harder side, but is ultimately the most culturally impactful soft magic system literature has ever seen.

Written by Robin Hobb, the sprawling Realm of the Elderlings series consists of several subseries (perhaps most notably the legendary Farseer trilogy). In it, an illegitimate royal prince's son, trained as an assassin and bound by forbidden magic, navigates a fractured world over the course of a massive 16-book epic. These are some of the fantasy books with the most interesting characters, the tightest plotting, and—of course—the best worldbuilding and magic-system writing.

Hobb's world features two primary magical forces: The Skill, a mental magic that connects minds over vast distances, and The Wit, a sensory magic that binds humans to animal companions. It seems simple on the surface, but Hobb constantly adds fascinating new layers to the system across those 16 novels, keeping the series' magic fresh, exciting, and thematically weighty throughout.

Almost universally recognized as the greatest and most influential fantasy novel of the entire 20th century, J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings was published in three separate volumes, but is technically all one single epic novel. For that matter, it's probably the best piece of epic fantasy ever written, and easily one of the best fantasy books of the 20th century. It follows Frodo, a hobbit who allies himself with a varied Fellowship to take a powerful, ancient ring and destroy it before it helps the Dark Lord Sauron regain his old power.

It's the gold standard of classic soft magic systems, and even though said system was technically introduced in The Hobbit and greatly expanded in The Silmarillion, it's The Lord of the Rings that sees the peak of its quality and entertainment value. Since the book is meant to operate so much like a modern myth, its magic feels like the magic of any other foundational mythology: deeply awe-inspiring, inherently tied to nature and the spiritual world, and impossible to fully pin down.

Ursula K. Le Guin was undeniably one of the most important authors in the whole history of speculative fiction, and the Earthsea Cycle is almost universally recognized as her magnum opus. This high fantasy book series consists of masterpiece after masterpiece, with some absolutely gorgeous prose and a clever subversion of traditional high fantasy tropes that has aged like fine wine.

But as great as virtually all aspects of the Earthsea Cycle, one of the most perfect fantasy book series ever, may be, many fans would agree that the magic system is the real star of the show. Rooted in disciplines like linguistics and Taoist philosophy, Earthsea's soft magic system is based on names, balance, and nature. It's deeply philosophical, elegantly constructed, and nothing short of gorgeous.

#3456. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3455. Henry Cavill's The Witcher Replacement Has One Major Advantage Over Geralt Of Rivia

After starring on Netflix's The Witcher for three seasons, Henry Cavill's big role in an upcoming movie is the perfect next step in the actor's career, with one major advantage over his previous fantasy part. Before Liam Hemsworth took over the role of Geralt in season 4, Cavill had become synonymous with the character, making his exit so upsetting.

The world of The Witcher is bigger than any one cast member. The Witcher: Sirens of the Deep had a different Geralt, voiced by Doug Cockle, and built on a legacy that lasted even longer than Cavill had in the part. Cockle previously voiced Geralt of Rivia in all three The Witcher video games, helping to craft the character onscreen.

Considering that the games themselves informed much of the look and feel of the series, and were themselves drawn from The Witcher novels, that world is actually large enough to last without Henry Cavill. And the actor's talents have now been pointed toward a perfect role, with a character who has one major advantage over Geralt of Rivia.

Cavill's career in Hollywood is sure to be long and full of fantastic roles, but this upcoming project could become a defining film for the star.

After having played such iconic roles as Superman and Sherlock Holmes, his new take on another popular and beloved part could be the perfect chance for Cavill to do something truly unique, thanks to an incredible ability.

Henry Cavill will star in the upcoming remake of Highlander, where his lead character, Connor MacLeod, will have a power that no other characters in Cavill's past have. Connor MacLeod is an Immortal and serves as the center of the story as the titular Highlander, who is set to one day fight for The Prize.

While there is an inherent tension to Connor's existence, as captured by the original 1986 Highlander film's popular quote, "There can be only one", this is still an incredible power.

Born in the 16th century in Scotland, Connor has spent centuries exploring the Earth and training as a swordsman in order to one day be able to fight to become the last of his kind.

Connor has possessed some powers in addition to his immortality. During the Quickening, when an Immortal is killed, generally by another Immortal, a surge of energy escapes their body, allowing the victor to absorb the strength and memories of their fallen foe. This adds to a powerset that also includes enhanced regeneration.

Still, even with all of Connor's fantastic abilities, the character is important to compare against the roles that Cavill has played in the past. And while Geralt of Rivia might not be immortal, he does possess some fantastic skills that might make him even stronger than Connor could ever hope to be.

Geralt of Rivia actually shares some similarities in his powers with Connor MacLeod. While not hampered by a connection to a race of Immortals, which is itself an asset to Geralt's mortality, The Witcher's protagonist also has the benefit of slow aging, as well as tremendous skills in regeneration and healing.

Geralt, another trained swordsman, has greater speed, skill, and reflexes than Connor has generally been depicted as having. A fantastic tracker with elevated senses, Geralt has also been mutated in several ways that contribute to his incredibly enhanced physical powers of movement, fighting, and more.

If Geralt of Rivia and Connor MacLeod ever met in battle, it is hard to say exactly who would emerge triumphant, and much of that will depend on how the upcoming film depicts Connor. However, the more battle-hardened and practiced Geralt of Rivia would likely have at least a small advantage over his Highlander foe.

Regardless, both characters are excellent parts for Henry Cavill. And while The Witcher will continue to live on without him in some form, even after the Netflix series ends, this new and thrilling story of a rebooted Highlander is only about to get started.

#3454. 8 Upcoming Sci-Fi Movies, Ranked by Hype

2026 has been a strong and packed year for sci-fi cinema, anchored by both major box office sensations and indie hits. And now, the last stretch of the year is set to get bigger and bolder with some massive blockbusters that are arriving just before the year ends. From blockbuster cosmic spectacles to thought-provoking, human stories, and a brand-new Star Wars film starring Ryan Gosling, there are several highly anticipated sci-fi films to look forward to in the coming months.

2026 has seen several sci-fi hits so far, and the last weeks of the year will see the genre gearing up for an explosive finish with Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, arriving just in time for the holidays. Also arriving at the same time is Marvel’s mammoth cinematic event Avengers: Doomsday, bringing the entire MCU together (one last time?). But this streak does not end here and will continue in the coming year. 2027 will also be the year when centenarian Mel Brooks returns with a Spaceballs sequel after four decades. So without further ado, here’s your guide to the most notable upcoming sci-fi movies, ranked by hype.

Directed by Brad Bird and written by Bird and Matthew Robbins, Ray Gunn is an animated sci-fi mystery set in a gigantic city called Metropia, in a retro-futuristic universe where humans and various interplanetary species coexist. The story follows the titular human private detective who takes up a murder case involving a famous multimedia star named Venus Nova, whose stardom is threatened by a scandal. The film stars the voices of Sam Rockwell as Ray and Scarlett Johansson as Venus, with Tom Waits, Matt Berry, Bobby Cannavale, Michelle Rodriguez, Alan Tudyk, and Patton Oswalt as notable characters.

Ray Gunn premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival, where it received strong praise for its animation, action scenes, and voice acting, particularly from Rockwell, Johansson, and Waits. As is evident from its trailer, the film is a high-octane stunner, passionately inspired by Hollywood noir classics, joining the ranks of Brad Bird’s other acclaimed animated films like The Incredibles and Ratatouille. Following its theatrical release, Ray Gunn will also make its streaming debut on Netflix on December 18, 2026.

Mel Brooks’ classic satirical space opera film series returns after four decades with a brand-new sequel, Spaceballs: The New One, which picks up forty years after the events of the original 1987 film. In the upcoming film, villain Dark Helmet has returned, while Lone Starr is in hiding and Queen Vespa attends to her royal duties, so Prince Starburst, Vespa's son, and Destiny, a royal advisor, are tasked with finding Lone Starr and other allies to defeat the new threat. Brooks, Rick Moranis, Bill Pullman, George Wyner, and Daphne Zuniga reprise their roles from the previous film, with Lewis Pullman, Keke Palmer, Josh Gad, and Anthony Carrigan as new characters.

The new Spaceballs comes from director Josh Greenbaum, whom fans might know from films like Strays and The Dink, and is written by Josh Gad, Dan Hernandez, and Benji Samit. An '80s cult classic comedy, Spaceballs is among the best sci-fi parody films ever made and a major highlight of Mel Brooks’ career and legacy. Much like the first film, Spaceballs: The New One will mainly spoof the Star Wars franchise but is also expected to be a meta comedy about the modern nostalgia-obsessed culture, massive cinematic universes, and the rising trend of reboot films.

Directed by Eric Guillon, Claire Dodgson, and Jonathan del Val, Not Alone is an animated sci-fi rom-com centering on two scientists and clueless romantics, Joe and Fran, who are devising the world’s first plant-fueled rocket. When Joe finds himself harboring three alien fugitives stranded on Earth, he must figure out a way to send them home while also winning Fran’s love before it is too late. Timothée Chalamet and Selena Gomez voice Joe and Fran, respectively, with Brett Goldstein, Rob Brydon, Jamie Demetriou, and Diane Morgan voicing other key characters.

Not Alone marks Illumination’s first original feature since 2023’s Migration and the studio’s first romantic comedy, as well as its first feature film of 2027. As seen in the trailer, the film promises a wild, intergalactic adventure with adorable aliens and a charming love story at its heart that would appeal to everyone. While the film bears Illumination’s signature visual tone and style that has become synonymous with blockbuster animated franchises, Not Alone marks a shift from the studio’s traditional storytelling style, which is generally targeted towards a younger audience.

Directed by Grant Sputore, Godzilla x Kong: Supernova is a sequel to Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire and serves as the sixth film in Legendary Pictures’ Monsterverse franchise. In the film, Godzilla and Kong must team up once again, this time against a cosmic threat in the form of SpaceGodzilla. Dan Stevens reprises his role as Trapper from The New Empire, with Kaitlyn Dever, Jack O'Connell, Alycia Debnam-Carey, Matthew Modine, and Delroy Lindo as new characters, as well as Sam Neill in one of his final film roles.

Godzilla x Kong: Supernova marks the 40th film in the Godzilla franchise and the 14th film in the King Kong franchise, shifting the franchise into cosmic sci-fi territory. SpaceGodzilla first appeared in the 1994 film Godzilla vs. SpaceGodzilla as the main antagonist and is depicted as a crystalline, mutated clone of Godzilla. While the reappearance of two prehistoric behemoths in another earth-shattering monster war is what makes the upcoming film most hyped, Godzilla x Kong: Supernova is expected to dive deeper into the human-monster coexistence dynamic as well.

Directed by Francis Lawrence, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the Hunger Games film series and an adaptation of Suzanne Collins' dystopian novel of the same name. Set 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, Sunrise on the Reaping revolves around a young Haymitch Abernathy, who is selected to compete in the 50th Hunger Games and fight to the death in a televised spectacle. The film stars Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, and Elle Fanning as key characters.

Sunrise on the Reaping serves as a sequel to The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes and a prequel to the 2012 film The Hunger Games, with Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson reprising their roles from the films. The film premiered in London in October 2026, where it had an overwhelmingly positive reception, with critics praising Zada’s breakout performance and hailing the movie as the best installment in the Hunger Games film series so far. Franchise fans are sure to love the film’s mature and politically charged narrative of cruelty, grief, and rebellion.

Among the most anticipated films in the Star Wars franchise is the upcoming Star Wars: Starfighter, starring Ryan Gosling. Directed by Shawn Levy and written by Jonathan Tropper, the film is set five years after the events of 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker and follows Gosling’s cynical rogue pilot Kade Auberon, who is hired to escort a mysterious, Force-sensitive boy across a dangerous, lawless galaxy. The film also stars Amy Adams, Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Flynn Gray, Aaron Pierre, and Daniel Ings.

Star Wars: Starfighter is a standalone Star Wars film with no ties to the Skywalker Saga or legacy characters from the previous films. Produced by Levy and Lucasfilm, the adventure film does not require any prior knowledge of the franchise and its decades-spanning lore, making it accessible to general audiences while keeping the classic Star Wars magic intact. Starfighter is scheduled to release in May 2027, coinciding with the 50th anniversary of the first Star Wars film, which was released in May 1977.

Denis Villeneuve’s epic space opera franchise returns this December with its final chapter, Dune: Part Three, based on Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah. Set nearly two decades after Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides seized control of the Imperium, the film sees the emperor forced to face the true cost of power and the fate of those he loves as old allies and a long-lost love return and new enemies emerge. Most of the stars from the previous films reprise their roles, including Zendaya, Florence Pugh, Jason Momoa, Josh Brolin, Rebecca Ferguson, and Javier Bardem, with Robert Pattinson, Anya Taylor-Joy, and Isaach de Bankolé as new characters.

Dune: Part Three is one of the most anticipated sci-fi films of 2026 and marks the final installment in Villeneuve’s Dune film trilogy that began in 2021. Before its premiere, the film won the Golden Trailer Award for the original score by Hans Zimmer, who also composed the music for the previous two films. Alongside high-stakes battles and visceral action pieces, Dune: Part Three is expected to be much darker and more intimate than the previous Dune films, serving as a deconstruction of the classic tragic hero’s journey.

A much-awaited cinematic phenomenon, Anthony and Joe Russo’s Avengers: Doomsday is the 39th MCU film featuring the titular characters from Marvel Comics and a kind of sequel to 2019’s Avengers: Endgame. Intended to be a super-superhero film like never before, the new film brings together the Avengers, New Avengers, Fantastic Four, X-Men, and Wakandans, as well as other iconic characters to stop Doctor Doom and the collapse of the multiverse. Pretty much every MCU star is expected to appear in the film, including Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers / Captain America. Robert Downey Jr.’s return to the MCU in the new role of Victor von Doom is something to look forward to as well.

Arguably the most hyped film of 2026, Avengers: Doomsday is set up to be a massive showcase of the MCU’s legendary characters from all the previous films in an action-packed, CGI spectacle. For fans who might need a refresher on the characters, the multiverse mechanics, and how their arcs come together, Marvel Studios and Disney+ have curated an official "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" watch guide featuring a much smaller, streamlined list of essential titles. Releasing in the US following its UK premiere in December 2026, Doomsday will be followed by Avengers: Secret Wars, arriving in 2027.

#3452. 6 R-Rated Superhero Shows Better Than The Boys

The superhero landscape looked very different back in 2019 before The Boys came around, as despite there being a fair few R-rated projects on the market, none were as crude or graphic as Prime Video's mega hit. Alongside putting a completely different spin on the genre by having mainly evil superheroes, The Boys also parodied Marvel, DC, and various other franchises.

However, with The Boys ending earlier in 2026, it left a big gap in the world of R-rated superhero shows, and while spinoffs such as Vought Rising and The Boys: Mexico will continue this universe, things simply won't be the same without the main series. Fortunately, there is already an abundance of great competitors out there.

Originally, it looked like Gen V would be The Boys' replacement before being canceled, but if you are looking for R-rated hits that are even better than anything this violent franchise produced, these six projects are definitely worth checking out.

Despite lasting just two seasons, The Punisher feels like a complete series that extends Frank Castle's story after first appearing in Daredevil. Getting to learn about the tragic events that turned him from a loving husband and father to a merciless killing machine is fascinating, and The Punisher certainly doesn't pull any punches with its violence.

As we've seen in the 2004 movie, characterizing Frank isn't always easy, as without the right nuance, he can feel empty and hard to connect with. However, Jon Bernthal delivers an outstanding performance that shows the humanity behind this vigilante, making it easier to root for him, despite not always agreeing with his actions.

The first season comes across as more personal, with Frank getting vengeance on those who were responsible for the death of his family, and the supporting cast is a key part of his journey. Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Amber Rose Revah, and Ben Barnes all do a great job with their respective characters, and while it can be an uncomfortable watch at times, The Punisher's story is ultimately very satisfying.

Season 2 presents a different vibe, with Giorgia Whigham's Amy Bendix bringing out the more fatherly side of Frank. Not only does he risk his own life to protect Amy, but he stands up for injustice outside his own personal grievances, with the final scene showing him fully embracing his Punisher persona.

Considering the character has been brought back as part of the MCU and even had his own special, it's clear Bernthal made a big impact as the Punisher, and the show successfully delivers exactly the type of brutal action needed to make it an all-time great that eclipses The Boys.

With James Gunn and Peter Safran stepping down from their leadership positions at DC Studios, the future of Lanterns is uncertain, but after just one season, it has already made a huge impression. Culturally, the show was massive, as it rejuvenated interest in the Green Lantern mythos and had people constantly bringing new theories and memes every week.

Sure, it definitely proved divisive as comic readers had major issues with the character and story direction, but as a whole, Lanterns was incredibly popular. The season 1 finale pulled in over 10 million viewers in just three days, and even those who hate the show can't deny how exceptional Kyle Chandler is as Hal Jordan, with Aaron Pierre shining opposite him.

Even though the series leans more into the mystery and detective genre than classic superhero elements, there are still several fun action sequences that definitely qualify it as a superhero project over something like The Penguin. Additionally, Lanterns sets up John Stewart to be more powerful in Man of Tomorrow, which should make up for the lack of major fight scenes.

It's rare that a modern show makes such a seismic impact in just nine episodes, but in terms of quality and consistency, Lanterns trumps The Boys, despite the latter having higher highs. The desire for a second season and Hal's return highlights how good the HBO series really is, and hopefully there's still a future for this surprise hit.

Much like Lanterns, Peacemaker's future is uncertain, even more so since James Gunn directed it, but it seems like season 2 was always planned to be the last anyway. Still, in just 16 episodes, Peacemaker manages to turn a bunch of obscure and original characters into fan favorites who audiences became 100% invested in.

John Cena's Peacemaker first appeared in 2021's The Suicide Squad, and while he was originally portrayed as arrogant and overconfident, viewers came around to him until he betrayed Rick Flag. That made centering a show around him extremely risky, yet Cena delivers a career-high performance full of emotion and vulnerability, adding so much depth to this anti-hero.

With an absolutely phenomenal cast for support, the series really thrives in its character work, making it almost essential that they return in future DCU projects. Both seasons feel incredibly different as they take place under completely different hierarchies, yet Gunn's vision allowed them to connect and achieve a similar quality.

Once again, it's a show that had people talking every week, predicting what would happen next, and somehow, people managed to guess season 2's most outlandish twist. At its core, Peacemaker is fun, hilarious, brutal, and surprisingly deep, cementing it as one of the greatest live-action superhero shows of the 21st century.

Its killer soundtrack only gives it more personality, and it has two of the best superhero show opening credits ever made, showing how much care was put into crafting this legendary series.

After the highly underrated 2009 movie, it wasn't clear how much legs the Watchmen franchise had in the highly competitive superhero market, but the TV show that premiered a decade later didn't disappoint. The series follows mostly different characters than the film, creating a unique spectacle, but one that is every bit entertaining.

Even though it's an original story, the tone and visuals capture what made the comics so great, and it isn't afraid to dive into culturally relevant topics. It tackles issues like racism in a mature manner, while having a compelling direction that isn't easy to predict, keeping viewers on their toes throughout all nine episodes.

Like the other entries on this list, the acting is top drawer, with Jeremy Irons standing out as the unhinged Ozymandias. The score is also worth mentioning, since it helps create the moody tone that makes Watchmen so gritty. That said, the show isn't afraid to get a little goofy at times either, with the humor separating it from DC's usual brand of comedy.

The story ties together nicely, and while the ending is packed, Watchmen still sticks the landing, making it no surprise it's so widely celebrated. It won 11 Emmys and was nominated for 26 in total, emphasizing the quality of this limited series, which didn't overstay its welcome.

Over 10 years ago, Daredevil debuted on Netflix, and to this day, many still see it as the greatest superhero show ever made. As a blind lawyer by day and a ruthless vigilante at night, Matt Murdock is the perfect protagonist for a dark, bloody show, and the three-season masterpiece couldn't have portrayed him any better.

Matt possesses all the charm and charisma needed to make him instantly likable, yet his disability and tragic origins cement him as a true underdog. Luckily, Foggy Nelson and Karen Page act as the optimal allies for him, which makes it all the more heartbreaking when he pushes them away, even if it's supposed to be for selfless reasons.

The drama is ever-present, and the choreography is perhaps still the gold standard for superhero projects, with that iconic one-shot hallway brawl remaining relevant all these years later. That's not to overlook Frank Castle's prison fight or the office brawl between Daredevil and Bullseye in season 3.

Speaking of Bullseye, he and Kingpin were so good that they both returned for Daredevil: Born Again with the same actors, confirming these villains were irreplaceable. Daredevil also has fantastic cinematography, with vibrant colors and shots helping forge an identity that the Disney+ show couldn't replicate, despite trying its best.

Between the fantastic cast, gripping storylines, flawless editing, and all the other qualities Daredevil possesses, it's no surprise it has such a stellar reputation. It is a superhero show that changed the genre forever, and while The Boys did the same, it simply doesn't measure up to Netflix's Daredevil.

While The Boys deserves a lot of credit for breaking the traditional Marvel and DC dominance by becoming one of the biggest superhero shows of the past decade, its Prime Video competitor did the same and is even better. Invincible arrived two years after The Boys, but the animated hit is far more consistent, and still has a healthy future ahead of it.

As a faithful comic adaptation, Invincible retells the story of Robert Kirkman's original series, albeit with some tweaks and additions. Its vast roster of characters is among its biggest strengths, as alongside having a fleshed-out, complex protagonist, there are so many wonderful heroes, villains, and other supporting allies that make the universe feel alive.

There is no holding back when it comes to fights either, as the gory injuries make even The Boys look tame at times. Invincible also does a great job of adding genuinely hilarious gags and jokes into its otherwise serious narrative, which is far less shocking or in your face than its Prime Video counterpart.

Some of its very best episodes have near-perfect ratings on IMDb, putting them among the greatest in TV history, and mixed with a fantastic soundtrack, A-list cast, and constant drama, there is no denying that Invincible is a better superhero series than The Boys.

The fact that the show managed to overcome its biggest weakness by shortening the gap between seasons to release regularly means it is bound to keep getting better, and with several seasons still to come for Invincible, it deserves to be recognized as one of the best in the genre.

#3451. India Love Apologizes To People Offended By Comments About Gay Friend

Influencer India Love is apologizing to anyone offended by her recent comments about wanting her gay friend to stop being gay.

India says she is getting death threats after a clip of her from her live stream talking about the topic went viral this week. She said she is still friends with her friend, despite people thinking she cut him off.

She claimed her gay friend reached out to her after the clip went viral and was also confused by the backlash. India said she didn’t mean to offend people … and said she’s just a follower of Jesus Christ.

#3450. ‘Elsbeth’ Is Ready to Play a ‘Ted Lasso’ Star’s Game in First Look at This Week’s New Episode

After venturing into country club society and solving a murder on the green involving Nat Faxon, it's time for Elsbeth to head somewhere a little more fun. Season 4 has already been a busy one for the pink-clad sleuth, between not just solving murders but helping plan her son Teddy's (Ben Levi Ross) wedding. What better area in all of New York City, then, for a day of fun than the legendary amusement district that is Coney Island? Episode 5 of CBS' hit murder mystery procedural will take Carrie Preston to the park where business once again awaits her in the world of competitive eating with a Ted Lasso star.

Titled "All About Eats," the episode unfolds in the aftermath of a deadly donut-eating competition after which a Coney Island champion dies under mysterious circumstances. Enter Elsbeth to follow the crumbs and find out who's responsible for the gastronomical crime. She soon finds a suspect in Cody Baxter, an up-and-coming eating star and superfan of the sport played by Tim Robinson's Detroiters partner, Sam Richardson. It appears he may have gotten a little too hungry for the crown and bit off a little more than he could chew to knock off his top opponent, but to expose him, Elsbeth will have to play at his game.

Ahead of the premiere this Thursday, Collider can exclusively share a new sneak peek that sees Elsbeth running into Cody on the famed Coney Island boardwalk, where he works as an "independent contractor." He doesn't like being called a "carnie" because it gives the impression he's "weird," but he doesn't exactly do a great job of breaking the negative connotation in their awkward conversation.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Season 4 of Elsbeth has been just as star-studded as ever, with Richardson adding to a lineup that has thus far included Nicole Scherzinger, Nicholas Braun, the aforementioned Faxon, and even an appearance from New York Knicks star OG Anunoby. However, while the series still has more guests from its first round to get through, even more big names have recently signed on to join Robert and Michelle King's procedural. The Big Bang Theory star Simon Helberg will be one of the new suspects, playing a Revolutionary War reenactor whose spot is threatened by an up-and-comer. He'll be followed by SNL alum Molly Shannon, who plays a rising star creator of a female superhero, and Manchester by the Sea star Lucas Hedges as the founder of a prediction market. With them helping to fill out the rest of the season, Elsbeth is showing no signs of slowing down as the fall season winds into winter.
