#3425. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Now that I’ve flipped my calendar to November, I’m counting down to Christmas and planning how I’ll decorate my home.

However, I don’t stick to the usual festive tree and decorative lights; I always rely on seasonal houseplants to bring vibrant life into the mix. Apart from my Christmas cactus, a poinsettia is a must-have — it’s basically Christmas in a pot.

Step into any garden center in mid-November, and you can’t miss a sea of crimson. Poinsettias have officially arrived and are the bright spark of color that signals the holiday season is near. But picking up a pot before Santa slides down the chimney comes with a risk. Choose the wrong plant now, and you could be left with a wilted stem by Christmas morning.

So how do you choose the perfect poinsettia so it still looks good when Santa arrives in December? Here, David Denyer, flower expert at Eflorist, shares how to choose a poinsettia in November so it creates a perfect display right through to the New Year.

Whether you’re picking a poinsettia for yourself or as a festive gift, Denyer advises checking the center of the colored leaves, known as bracts. “You’ll see small yellow-green buds, which are the true flowers. If these are still tight and unopened, your plant is fresh and will last much longer.”

Did you know?The colored sections on a poinsettia look like flowers, but they’re bracts, often called modified leaves. The red ‘petals’ have developed to attract pollinators to the tiny flowers in the center. Bougainvilleas and passion flowers are two other plants with bracts that are easy to mistake for petals.

When you go to buy a poinsettia, Denyer says there are two red flags to watch for. He advises against buying a poinsettia with drooping, yellowing or missing leaves. It’s not a healthy start.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There’s another danger sign to watch for before buying this festive plant. Denyer adds, “Don’t choose plants that have been displayed outside shops or near automatic doors,” and he adds, “they’ll most likely be damaged by the cold draughts already.”

It appears that poinsettias prefer to be snug rather than chilly, so to keep your poinsettia protected, Denyer recommends, “Be sure to keep your poinsettias warm by wrapping them for the journey home; they really don’t like the cold.”

Once you’ve picked a healthy poinsettia, it needs to be treated just right to keep it looking its best, which is why it helps to know that this plant is used to sunny climates.

“Being native to Mexico, it makes sense that poinsettias love warmth and light, so placement is crucial,” says Denyer. “Select a bright room, ideally near a window where it can enjoy plenty of indirect light, but without its leaves touching the cold glass.”

They thrive in temperatures between 59-70°F (15–21°C), but they don’t like sudden changes, so he says, keep them away from draughty doorways, radiators, fireplaces and open windows, as they’ll struggle otherwise.

This attractive indoor watering can holds 35 oz of water and comes in sage green with a decorative wooden handle and a gooseneck spout. The durable stainless steel is leakproof, scratch resistant, and anti-corrosive.

According to Denyer a poinsettia will hold onto its color for at least six to eight weeks, so a plant brought in mid-November should see you through until the end of December. If you wait until December to buy your plant, it will keep going until the end of January.

There are four main stages can help you keep a poinsettia alive beyond the festive season. Here, Denyer explains what to do and when.

Late winterOnce the bracts begin to fade, gradually reduce watering and let the compost dry out a little more between drinks.

AprilCut the stems back to around 4 inches (10 cm) and keep the plant somewhere warm and bright.

MayWhen new growth appears, repot into fresh compost, then water regularly and feed every couple of weeks throughout summer.

FallFrom late September, give your plant around 14 hours of complete darkness each night for eight weeks. Covering it with a box or popping it in a cupboard overnight will do the trick. This short-day treatment triggers the colorful bracts to develop in time for Christmas.

#3422. 31 Years Later, The Line That Changed The X-Files Is Still A Work Of Genius

Faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones.  You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

The X-Files' impact on both the sci-fi genre and culture is arguably second only to that of Star Trek. Through Dana Scully, "The Scully Effect" encouraged more women to pursue careers in the sciences, while the iconic 90s sci-fi series popularized the monster-of-the-week format, which inspired later TV shows like Warehouse 13 and Supernatural. The X-Files' classic episodes were never predictable, but viewers knew to expect a lineup of monsters, mutants, out-of-control computers, and other paranormal phenomena with every season, until one season 3 episode expanded The X-Files' scope with two words.

The fourth episode of The X-Files' season 3 sees Mulder and Scully investigating a string of gory murders targeting psychics, when they come across the tormented Clyde Bruckman, who claims that he can see how everyone he ever meets will die. The premise initially sounded fairly standard for The X-Files, but the episode, "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose," contained a shocking twist. After Scully spends the episode trying to debunk Clyde's psychic powers, curiosity gets the better of her, and she asks him how she will die. Clyde responds, "you don't."

The line turned the series into an existential and spiritual mystery that had viewers discussing its implications for years afterward, even after The X-Files continued with its monster-of-the-week format for some time afterward. This moment, and the standout acting and directing kept "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" among the best X-Files episodes of all time, and the line's eventual payoff completed a four-year masterclass in suspense.

According to IMDb, "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" is The X-Files' top-rated episode, earning a 9.2/10 mark, and it attracted an audience of 15.38 million viewers. A few episodes of the show have not aged well, but "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" is still among the X-Files episodes that are considered masterpieces today. Written by Darin Morgan and directed by David Nutter, who would later go on to win an Emmy Award for Game of Thrones, the episode is extremely dark, verging into film noir territory, and many of the references are hidden tributes to cinema's silent film era.

The genius of the episode is not just in the plot, but the way Mulder and Scully are developed further as characters in ways that are not easy to achieve within a monster-of-the-week format. While remaining the show's skeptic, Scully has previously been sensitive to influence by psychics, with "Beyond the Sea" flipping her and Mulder's roles in the show. Now, she remains unconvinced by the psychic aspect but sees Clyde as a tragic and human figure, which allows her to set aside the cold and scientific demeanor she sometimes puts on, while Mulder treats him as a case study.

"Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" won The X-Files two Emmy Awards. Darin Morgan won Outstanding Writing in a Drama Series, while Peter Boyle (Clyde) won Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series.

The episode is full of tiny unpredictable scenes and surprises for viewers, introducing a dark comedy moment when Clyde heavily implies that Mulder will die during a sexual mishap, but it was Clyde's line to Scully that reportedly sent fans into a frenzy, with the "Immortal Dana Scully" theory being the inevitable result. It is a testament to the quality of the episode that it is remembered for so many factors, from the acting to the heartbreaking ending, despite delivering the line that changed The X-Files, even though this line was later revealed to be a misunderstanding.

Four years after Clyde Bruckman appeared to confirm Scully's immortality, the season 6 episode "Tithonus" reinforced this by having her survive against impossible odds. While investigating Alfred Fellig, a seemingly-immortal photographer on a mission to photograph Death, Scully is shot, yet Fellig takes her place. By this time, The X-Files had already begun making references to events in earlier seasons, tying its mythology together as the show moved away from the monster-of-the-week approach, and expanding its universe. However, this reference may not have been made had it not been for Clyde's line originally being misinterpreted.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

Chris Carter's Reddit AMA thread sees a fan ask him if Scully really is immortal, getting the reply, "Yes, it said so right in the show," but Darin Morgan has repeatedly explained that he had meant this line as a way for Clyde to be kind to Scully, knowing how she died, yet denying that she would. He told TVLine, "that was not my intention. That was something fans went crazy with — and they're free to go as crazy as they want." Immortal Scully or not, "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" remains one of The X-Files' must-watch episodes.

#3421. Steven Spielberg’s 10-Part Sci-Fi Thriller Is Perfect for ‘Person of Interest’ Fans

15 years ago, CBS delivered one of its best procedurals with Person of Interest. The series, which focuses on a mysterious "Machine" and a former Special Forces operative tasked by the Machine's creator to protect the people it identifies, perfectly blends a high concept sci-fi pitch with the standard procedural formula. Like Lost before it, Person of Interest saw a wake of similar shows premiering after its debut, most notably Almost Human. One series boasts the pedigree of being a direct sequel to one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century.

That series is Minority Report, which picks up in the aftermath of Steven Spielberg's sci-fi thriller. The Minority Report series follows Dash (Stark Sands), a former precognitive whose visions were used by the "Precrime" police department to stop crimes before they happen. Haunted by visions of murders yet to happen, Dash contacts Detective Lara Vega (Meagan Good) to help stop those crimes before they happen. Though it only lasted a single season, Minority Report had similar vibes to Person of Interest, including deep questions about the nature of justice.

Part of the draw of Minority Report is the dynamic between Dash and Vega, especially as she gets used to the fact that he can see the future and transitions into a normal life while still using his abilities to help others. The episode "The Present" is perhaps the strongest example of this dynamic at work, as Dash gets a flash of Vega's death and works to solve it while she deals with the unresolved matter of her father's death. Another element that makes Minority Report stand out is its approach to the future, especially since the series takes place 11 years after the movie. Spielberg was ahead of the curve by asking scientists what technology would look like in the 2050's, and showrunner Max Borenstein said he took a similar approach when envisioning his take on Minority Report.

"One of the refreshing things about the film is that it didn't posit a single catastrophic event that led to the future. It said, "50 years from now, what is the world going to look like?" And the answer was that the world is going to be good and bad in equal measure to today. We have horrible thing that happen in our world, so I don't think we need to conjure up an apocalypse on our show to have real stakes."

Minority Report would also continue to incorporate elements from the movie, including Dash's siblings Arthur (Nick Zano) and Agatha (Laura Reagan). Both of them have wildly different visions; while Arthur gains knowledge of people who are about to be murdered, Agatha ends up psychically stepping in their shoes, which is just as horrifying as it sounds. The duo ends up helping Dash and Vega, but they have to be careful, as mysterious forces are hunting all three precogs to use their abilities. If Person of Interest is a story about the dangers of unchecked technology, then Minority Report asks what the law will do to keep people safe.

Despite being based on one of Steven Spielberg's most iconic movies, and even boasting Spielberg as an executive producer, Minority Report only lasted a single season. The deck was stacked against it from the start, as Fox cut the first season's episode order from thirteen episodes to ten and had it airing in the same time slot as NBC's The Voice, which was at the height of its popularity. Bad reviews didn't help, either, as many critics felt that Minority Report lacked the spark of the movie that inspired it.

The cast and crew of Minority Report has managed to find success with other sci-fi projects. Max Borenstein helped kick off the MonsterVerse movies, Nick Zano would become an integral part of Legends of Tomorrow, and Li Jun Li would go on to headline buzzy projects like Sinners and Spider-Noir. Still, for a series that was about predicting the future, Minority Report never saw its own end coming.

#3416. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3415. The Best Ongoing Science Fiction Franchise Is A Secret To 99% Of Fans

Science fiction comics have no shortage of sprawling universes, but one of the most ambitious currently being built has taken an unusual route to reach readers. Three Worlds / Three Moons, or 3W/3M, is a shared science-fiction setting created by Jonathan Hickman, Mike del Mundo, Mike Huddleston, and Nick Spencer. It began online in 2021, inviting readers to follow the worldbuilding process as it happened rather than simply receiving a finished comic.

That approach has helped 3W/3M grow into something bigger than a conventional comic-book series. Its creators have developed thousands of pages of stories and lore, experimented with digital reading platforms, and built a community around the universe. Dark Horse's 2026 publishing partnership is bringing the project to a much wider comic-shop and bookstore audience, but the printed books are only one part of its appeal.

Hickman introduced the project on August 9, 2021, describing it as a "concept universe" rather than a single storyline. Individual characters, locations, histories, and comics would contribute to a larger whole. Its foundational conflict moves through recurring eras in which science and magic rise and fall, giving the setting room to support stories across vastly different periods.

The premise is deliberately wider than a single space-faring adventure. The worldbuilding ranges across Akva, Therra, and Heir, alongside three moons, with societies, belief systems, economies, and political structures that give each corner of the universe its own identity. The creators wanted those details established before individual plots needed them, so the world could feel as if it existed beyond any protagonist.

The original creative group brought together Hickman with artists del Mundo and Huddleston, whose visual and design work helped shape the setting from the ground up. Nick Spencer later joined the core team, while other writers and artists contributed individual systems and stories. The project was conceived as a place where different creative voices could build connected material, not simply as one writer's long-running serial.

That approach also explains why the series can feel different from a traditional monthly comic. Hickman wanted stories of varying lengths and formats, with releases appearing when the work was ready rather than being forced into a standard issue count. He was also interested in restoring surprise to comics publishing, letting readers encounter new stories and artwork without every release being mapped out through conventional previews.

Jonathan Hickman and Mike del Mundo's 64-page graphic novel

Jonathan Hickman's introduction to the universe

Further exploration of the setting's lore

Geography and locations across the three worlds and three moons

Historical events, stories, and additional lore

The audience was part of the plan from the beginning. In his launch essay, Hickman said the team wanted readers to have a front-row seat during the creation process, with meaningful input at certain stages. That did not mean turning every plot point into a vote or handing over authorship. Instead, the creators made the development of characters, environments, lore, and creative decisions unusually visible.

That transparency became a key part of 3W/3M's identity. Through online posts, the team shared comics alongside process material and conversations about how the universe was designed. Readers could see how visual ideas connected to cultural details, why a place appeared where it did, or how a society's rules influenced the stories set inside it. Worldbuilding became part of the entertainment, not disposable bonus material.

The move into wider print distribution began with Dark Horse's announcement in February 2026. The publisher brought the universe to the direct market with Foundations, a 32-page, magazine-sized one-shot released on July 8 for $6.99. Written by Hickman and Spencer, with art by del Mundo and Huddleston, it follows astronaut and explorer Tajo Vallar on a doomed expedition to a dormant moon, where he uncovers mysteries that reignite an ancient conflict. Foundations builds on earlier digital material, including Fable and Ruin, which introduced Tajo, but gives new readers a clear entry point that does not require navigating years of online posts.

Dark Horse followed that launch with three oversized hardcover sourcebooks announced on July 17, 2026: [SYSTEMS], [MAPS], and [HISTORIES]. Each is planned as a 200-page, 8.5-by-11-inch volume combining comics with reference material and lore. The first, [SYSTEMS], is scheduled for February 2, 2027, at $39.99. Its twelve stories and data pages examine Therran birth assessments, royal duels on Heir, pirate searches for the treasure Khor, and the lore surrounding the gods.

Astarion, Karlach, and other fan-favorite heroes are officially returning in 2027 with new adventures that expand the world of Baldur’s Gate 3.

[MAPS], due April 6, 2027, functions as an atlas, charting locations from Akva's Khor-rich waters to Therra's labyrinths and Heir's rougher districts. It also includes twelve stories, with contributors such as James Stokoe and Juni Ba. [HISTORIES] follows on June 1, 2027, collecting six comics with lore and data that establish the worlds' timeline. Together, the three books offer newcomers a structured introduction to the setting while giving longtime readers more context for its cultures, geography, and past.

#3413. 10 Greatest Disney Movies That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

In 1923, brothers Walt and Roy O. Disney founded the Walt Disney Company to create their own run of animated shorts. From such humble beginnings, Disney has now grown to become perhaps the largest media conglomerate in the world, having absorbed the likes of Lucasfilm, Marvel, and 20th Century Fox. Though they now have their hands in everything from live action movies to theme parks, they still put effort into their animated movies, though recent years have seen them eclipsed by studios like DreamWorks and Sony when it comes to creativity and effort.

Still, there's no denying Disney has created some of the most well-known and beloved movies of all time. Regardless of when they first released, these movies continue to delight new and old viewers thanks to their strong writing, iconic characters, catchy songs, and the sense of fun and classic "Disney Magic" that ties them all together.

Aladdin (Scott Weinger) is a street rat living in the city of Agrabah with his monkey Abu (Frank Welker), who longs for a life of wealth and luxury so that nobody will ever look down on him again. After he is arrested following a chance meeting with the rebellious Princess Jasmine (Linda Larkin), Aladdin is recruited by the Royal Vizier, Jafar (Jonathan Freeman), to go inside the Cave of Wonders (Frank Welker) and retrieve a magic lamp. Aladdin discovers that the lamp contains a genie (Robin Williams) who is bound to grant three wishes to whomever holds the lamp, which he plans to use to become a prince and woo Jasmine.

Aladdin is one of the best examples of Disney's ability to combine comedy with heartfelt storytelling. Williams' performance as the Genie is so iconic that it changed how animated films handle celebrity voice actors, but when not throwing out rapid-fire jokes, he has a very sincere relationship with Aladdin that plays into the movie's themes about self-acceptance and integrity. The rest of the film is also great too: Jaffar stands tall as one of Disney's best villains thanks to his charisma, the animation is colorful and stylistic, and the songs catchy and all key to the story and characters.

While sailing from England to Port Royal, Elizabeth Turner (Lucinda Dryzek and Kiera Knightly) helps to rescue a young boy named William Turner (Dylan Smith and Orlando Bloom) from a shipwreck, and takes his golden medallion so he wouldn't be mistaken for a pirate. Years later, Elizabeth is kidnapped by the dreaded pirate ship The Black Pearl, and learns that the medallion is the key to freeing them from their curse of undeath. To save her, Will recruits the help of Captain Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp), an eccentric pirate who has a history with the Pearl and its captain, Hector Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush).

Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl is the most successful live-action adaptation of Disney’s theme park rides, and spawned an entire franchise of swashbuckling adventure stories. The movie is the perfect combination of memorable characters, fast-paced sword fights, high-seas action, and creative storytelling that weaves mythology and real history. Of all the characters, Jack Sparrow easily stands out the most thanks to Depp's phenomenal performance, and has cemented himself as one of the most iconic pirates in pop-culture history.

Ariel (Jodi Benson) is the youngest daughter of the Sea King, Triton (Kenneth Mars), but, much to his frustration, she has a fascination with the surface world and regularly goes looking for human artifacts. One night, she rescues Prince Eric (Christopher Daniel Barnes) after his ship is caught in a storm, and falls deeply in love with him. The whole affair is overseen by the sea witch Ursula (Pat Carroll), who plans to use Ariel's emotional vulnerability in her plan to usurp control of the sea from Triton.

The Little Mermaid is the movie that kick-started Disney's Renaissance, an era where Disney became the undisputed king of pop-culture. Even today, the movie still captivates audiences with its Broadway-style musical numbers by Alan Menken and Howard Ashman, and the underwater world is so lavishly animated. Character wise, Ariel and Eric have a pretty solid romance thanks to the film giving them time to develop as a couple, Triton is a solid father who goes through an arch regarding letting his daughter live her own life, and Urusla is so deliciously evil with her showmanship and Carroll's bombastic voice.

When an evil queen (Lucille La Verne) learns that her stepdaughter, Snow White (Adriana Caselotti), is more beautiful than her, she tasks her huntsman (Stuart Buchanan) with killing her. The huntsman can't bring himself to do it and instead tells the princess to run into the woods and never return. With the help of woodland animals, Snow White arrives at a cottage inhabited by seven dwarfs, who agree to let her stay with them.

Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs is not just the first Disney film, but also the first animated feature film in North America, and the first cell-shaded animated feature film. The movie set the bar for how to do fairy tale adaptations, with a story that plays on the audience's emotions to pull them into the character's struggles, hopes, and ambitions. The queen also set a very high bar for Disney villains thanks to her majestic and commanding presence in her normal form, and the cackling, bombastic villainy she exews upon transforming into her grotesque hag form.

Deep in the woods on a spring's day, the son of a stag called the Great Prince of the Forest (Fred Shields) is born. Named Bambi (Bobby Stewart, Hardie Albright, John Sutherland, and Donnie Duunagan), he grows up in the care of his mother (Paula Winslowe) and makes friends with a rabbit named Thumper (Peter Behn, Tim Davis, and Sam Edwards) and a skunk nicknamed Flower (Stan Alexander, Tim Davis, and Sterling Holloway). However, things become more difficult as the seasons change, and a mysterious creature called Man comes to the forest.

Bambi has gone from being a financial failure on release to one of the most beloved and respected animated animal films. It avoids excessive anthropomorphization of its characters, which, combined with the more realistic animal designs, presents the movie more as a snapshot of the natural world than a proper narrative. Its backgrounds by Tyrus Wong are also some of the most stylistic in any Disney film, using watercolor patterns to create a forest that feels all the more realistic and mysterious.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

In an alternate 1940s where humans live alongside living cartoon characters, Eddie Valiant (Bob Hoskins) is a private detective who has fallen onto hard times after the death of his brother at the hands of a toon. The day after he photographs Jessica Rabbit (Kathleen Turner) playing patty cake with the owner of Toontown, Marvin Acme (Stubby Kaye), he learns that Jessica's husband, Roger (Charles Fleischer), apparently murdered Acme in a jealous rage. Roger, however, seeks out Eddie to prove his innocence and protect him from the psychotic judge of Toontown, Judge Doom (Christopher Lloyd).

Who Framed Roger Rabbit is a revolutionary movie that has some of the best examples of mixing animated characters into live-action footage. This is thanks to the incredible level of detail that went into their creation, from using strings to move items the toon characters would hold to actively changing the shading on the characters to reflect changes in lighting. Beyond its technical achievements, it's also a very solid mystery with a strong film noir aesthetic, and some terrific performances from Hoskins and Lloyd.

To repair Mickey Mouse's declining popularity, Walt conceived an animated short based on Paul Dukas' symphonic poem The Sorcerer's Apprentice. As the budget grew too big to justify, Walt decided to turn the project into a feature film that would combine multiple shorts based on classical music. Leopold Stokowski was brought on as conductor, and Deems Taylor served as Master of Ceremonies.

The result was Fantasia, an ambitious film that combined music and animation like never before or since. The Disney animators put their all into each segment, matching the music with everything from proper narratives to simple abstract shapes that might come to one's mind as they hear the music. Disney would try to make similar films, but none of them ever matched the artistic creativity of the original movie.

Frustrated that his children Jane (Karen Dotrice) and Michael (Matthew Garber) have driven off another nanny, George Banks (David Tomlinson) places an ad in the paper for a strict nanny who will set them right. The next day, a wind blows away all the women who came to apply, and George instead hires Mary Poppins (Dame Julie Andrews), a woman who flew in on an umbrella, and meets the requirements of a separate ad made by the kids. Mary is indeed stern with the kids as needed, but also takes them on fantastical adventures with the help of her handyman friend, Bert (Dick Van Dyke).

Mary Poppins was famously despised by the author of the original books, P. L. Travers, but to general audience, it is one of Disney's biggest successes. This is thanks to its ability to blend the fun, whimsical adventures that Mary Poppins takes the children through with the hard-hitting but relatable reality of a father trying to rebuild a relationship with his kids. The songs by The Sherman Brothers help to convey this wide spectrum of emotions, with one song in particular, "Feed the Birds," having the honor of being Walt Disney's favourite from any of his movies.

All the animals of the Pride Lands travel to Pride Rock to celebrate the birth of the lion cub Simba (Johnathan Taylor Thomas and Matthew Broderick), son of King Mufasa (James Earl Jones). As he grows, Simba is educated by his father about the importance of maintaining the circle of life, but the young cub is too focused on how exciting it will be when he has the throne. Unfortunately, his uncle Scar (Jeremy Irons) lusts after the throne himself, and makes an alliance with a clan of hyenas to eliminate both Simba and Mufasa so he can take it.

The Lion King began life as a side-project to fill a 1994 release slot while Disney's best talent worked on Pocahontas, but it has since gone down in history as one of the most beloved animated films, and the highest grossing traditionally-animated one. The movie uses bold colors, wide shots, and foreground tricks to make the African Savannah feel massive and epic in scale, which pairs well with the story's themes about duty, responsibility, and learning from the mistakes of the past. Scar is also widely regarded as one of the best Disney villains thanks to how seamlessly the animation by Andreas Deja mixes with Irons' performance, creating a cunning, vicious villain who actually gets further in his plans than most Disney antagonists.

After refusing to shelter an old woman during a storm, a spoiled prince (Robby Benson) is turned into a beast and told to find love and be loved in return before the last petal of an enchanted rose falls, or he and his staff shall be cursed forever. Ten years later, he imprisons an inventor named Maurice (Rex Everhart) who trespassed during a storm, and meets Maurice's daughter, Belle (Paige O'Hara), when she comes looking for him. Belle offers to take her father's place as the Beast's prisoner, and, though things don't start off the best, the two do eventually come to see that there is more to the other than first appears.

Beauty and the Beast overcame a brutal production to not only receive near-universal acclaim, but also become the first animated film to be nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture—and remains the only 2D animated film and the only one from when the Oscars had five nominees instead of ten. The reason for this success is how seamlessly the movie weaves the classic themes of the original fairy tale with an updated story that gives all the characters more developed personalities, resulting in a believable romance and both Belle and Beast ranking among Disney's best characters. The animation is also beautiful, the songs by Menken and Ashman iconic, and its message about change and seeing what lies beneath the surface is timeless.

#3412. UK Celebrity Who Fought to Hide Sex Misconduct Allegations Unmasked

The mystery celebrity who spent weeks fighting to keep his name secret amid explosive sexual misconduct allegations has finally been unmasked ... and it's author David Walliams.

The popular British children's book author was previously identified only as "PPT" in court proceedings ... as he battled to stop two major news outlets from revealing his identity and publishing allegations against him. Walliams is also an actor and comedian who starred in the BBC sketch series "Little Britain" and "Come Fly With Me."

As TMZ previously reported ... the celebrity was accused of using his fame and influence to pursue inappropriate and exploitative sexual relationships with numerous girls and young women over the years ... allegations he has denied.

In an hour-long documentary released by ITN, a woman identified as "Alex" recalls meeting Walliams at a "Little Britain" signing in London in 2004 ... when she was just 15 and he was 32. She claims he immediately called her attractive and stared intensely into her eyes.

Another woman alleges Walliams sexually assaulted her at his home when she was 15 ... claiming he kissed her, lifted her shirt and touched her breast with his mouth before attempting to put her hand down his pants. She says she pulled away and told him no.

We also first reported, prior to his identity being revealed, Walliams was pulled from an upcoming UK film project, with a source close to production for "The Road to Nevermore" telling TMZ he was removed from the project after the allegations surfaced and scrubbed from their IMDb profile.

His attorneys argued that making the allegations public could have deadly consequences ... warning he was at serious risk of dying by suicide if his name was revealed.

But lawyers for ITN and The Guardian pushed back ... arguing the allegations were too important to keep hidden and that his mental health concerns should be addressed by medical professionals, not by silencing the press.

Tuesday morning, Judge Matthew Nicklin rejected the celebrity's attempt to block publication ... though his identity remained protected temporarily while a possible appeal was considered.

The legal battle also sparked a wave of online speculation ... prompting Nicklin to warn the public against trying to identify the mystery man, with anyone violating the court order potentially facing jail time.

Now, after weeks of secrecy and courtroom drama ... the mystery surrounding his identity is finally over.

#3411. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

The Samsung Galaxy S27 series is coming, and we've already started hearing a bunch of rumors about what the four upcoming phones might have to offer. The latest leak to appear online comes from SammyGuru, which features what is claimed to be camera specs for the entire S27 series. Sadly some of them are fairly disappointing.

The Galaxy S27 and S27 Plus are tipped to come with the exact same cameras that we're used to. This means they'll have a 50MP main camera powered by either a Sony IMX955 or Samsung S5KGNG sensor — both of which are available on the Galaxy S26 series. The Ultrawide is expected to be the 12MP Sony IMX564, which has been in use since the Galaxy S2series.

Resolution isn't specified for the selfie or telephoto cameras, only that they'll rely on a Samsung S5K3K1 with 3x optical zoom, and either the Samsung S5K3LU or Sony IMX874 for the front camera. Presumably, given what's happening with the other two lenses, we should expect a 10MP telephoto and 12MP selfie camera.

As for the S27 Ultra and S27 Pro, we're looking at a 200MP main camera, with the same Samsung S5KHP6 sensor on both models. That isn't the same sensor as the S26 Ultra (the S5KHP2), so it'll be interesting to see how things actually change. The Ultrawide will once again retain the 50MP resolution, utilizing a Samsung S5KJN3 or Sony IMX855 sensor.

Again that is the same on both phones, and the selfie camera follows that pattern with a shared Samsung S5K2P5 sensor offering 16MP resolution — a noticeable upgrade from the 12MP selfie camera on the S26 Ultra.

The telephoto lens is where things change. The S27 Ultra will reportedly have a 5x optical zooming camera powered by Sony IMX855 or Samsung S5KJN3, though resolution isn't specified. The Pro, on the other hand, utilizes the 3x Samsung SK53LD camera. This is the same sensor used by the S26 Ultra's secondary telephoto lens, which suggests it will have 10MP resolution.

So much for the rumors of a 50MP telephoto lens with 3.5x optical zoom. I figured that was too good to be true.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

If these specs are to be believed, there isn't going to be much difference between the cameras on the Pro and Ultra models. While this has me worried that the Pro will inevitably start cannibalizing the market from the Ultra, it does make some sense for people who want a powerful phone that's a little more compact than the gargantuan 6.9-inch Ultra models.

If a report from ETNews is to be believed, Samsung is going to be betting big on both phones. It's claimed that Samsung is setting aside 70% of its S27 production capacity for the Pro and Ultra models. That apparently translates to 18 million Galaxy S27 Ultras and between seven and eight million S27 Pros. The entire lineup will reportedly be around 35 million units, with the S27 and S27 Plus taking up the remaining nine to 10 million devices.

As Android Authority notes, the Galaxy S26 Ultra accounted for around 50% of this year's production capacity with Samsung reportedly producing the same 18 million units. In other words, it looks like Samsung is hoping the Pro model will offer enough to entice people that would otherwise buy the two cheapest Galaxy S phones.

The appeal of the Galaxy S27 Pro is that it offers more Ultra-style features for a lower price tag. Though to save on costs, some of those features will be cut. That's why the S27 Pro is expected to come with the 10MP telephoto lens, smaller 6.5-inch display and won't have a built-in S Pen.

However, the popularity of the new phone is almost certainly going to depend on the price. With prices rising across the board, and a rumor that the S27 series could suffer another price hike, there may be more of an appetite for cheaper devices even if it means losing out on the ultra-premium features and hardware in the process.

Then again, judging from the reaction to the Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, there's no shortage of people willing to pay a premium for their phones. So we'll just have to wait and see how this all plays out come January.

#3408. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3407. 'Chimp Crazy' Tonka is Safe After Florida Floods

The Florida sanctuary where beloved chimpanzee Tonka lives has been rocked by floods ... but the "Chimp Crazy" star is safe and sound.

Dan Mathews, Director of Events and Special Projects for Save the Chimps, tells TMZ … Save the Chimps got 19 inches of rain in 12 hours.

Mathews tells us ... all the chimps were brought inside except one named Kaleb. He says they weren’t able to get to him during the flooding and have been giving him items via drone.

We're told Tonka rode out the storm alongside 15 other chimps in the care house, and had a blast hanging out with fellow chimp, Kippy.

While the chimps are all doing just fine in the wake of the wild weather, Mathews tells TMZ the sanctuary's got a lot of damage.

He says Save the Chimps hasn't seen such intense flooding for the 25 years it's been in Fort Pierce.

The sanctuary's still assessing the damage, but Mathews estimates they're looking at over $100K in damage ... and they're turning to the public for financial help.

He says they need to re-surface the road around the property, fill in sinkholes, repair their buggy, replace their golf carts, repair roofs, re-landscape several parts of the refuge, and more.

He says the rain stopped on Tuesday and the water's gone down ... but it still hasn't gone away.

#3406. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3405. Michael Jackson: Blame Game Going On In Accusers' Battle Over Alleged Childhood Abuse

The legal battle between the entities in control of Michael Jackson's estate and the two men who claim they were sexually abused by the King of Pop is heating up ... and there's a lot of finger-pointing.

A Los Angeles judge sided with accusers Wade Robson and James Safechuck's move to stop Michael Jackson’s team from adding new arguments to their defense ... but did allow them the chance to amend their documents to reargue the point.

The lawyers for MJ's side were trying to amend their answers to the men's complaints so they could argue others are responsible for the alleged abuse of Wade and James ... and not MJ's companies.

In the filing, the lawyers adamantly dispute that Michael ever abused a child ... and point out Wade and James, and their parents, were among MJ's strongest supporters until well after his death.

The companies argued that, even if a jury believes the allegations of abuse, they should be allowed to make the argument that others who were not sued should also potentially be on the hook for damages ... including third parties who they say encouraged and facilitated Wade and James' friendships with the late singer.

Wade and James argued the defendants waited too long to add the argument ... and asked for the request to amend the suit be denied.  The court ended up denying the companies' motion to amend the complaint at this stage of the case ... but left the door open for them to file a renewed motion for leave to amend if appropriate down the line.

As TMZ first reported, Wade and James are seeking over $400 million in damages from MJ's companies.

Wade claims MJ abused him when he hung out with him after meeting him when he was 7 ... and James says he met the singer while working on a Pepsi commercial in 1986 and claims he was abused in the years after the introduction.

#3403. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, according to price-tracking tools, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3402. Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Personal Finance feature

Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

“Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself,” Anthropic says. “With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Similar to ChatGPT’s finances feature, Claude’s new capabilities essentially give you a way to use chat as a way to make sense of your finance data. It can also present data in dashboards, calendars, and more.

Given the importance of security, here’s what Anthropic has to say regarding the new finance feature and Claude:

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That’s where you agree to its terms and approve Claude’s read-only access, so Claude doesn’t ask for or see your bank password.

A slow-draining or completely blocked kitchen drain is a major frustration you don’t need. Besides smelling unpleasant and potentially damaging your pipes, it slows you down as you wait for your sink to empty.

Over time, warm fats, cooking oils and butter innocently slip down the drain, but instead of fully descending, they cool and solidify. Before long, that solid grease is catching hold of other small morsels of food, stopping them from making a clear escape.

But before you try to clear your blocked kitchen drain with a harsh chemical cleaner or call in a plumber, there’s an alternative method you can try.

Cleaning expert Lynsey Crombie, known as the Queen of Clean, recommends using a cooking staple to remove grease from kitchen drains. While this common ingredient is used to season food, it also dissolves grease.

And she adds, “Salt absorbs grease and liquid, lifts stubborn stains (even red wine), and is mildly antibacterial — making it perfect for soaking kitchen sponges or scrubbing chopping boards.”

In the social post, she shows herself pouring table salt down her kitchen drain, then boiling water.

A post shared by Lynsey Queen Of Clean (@lynsey_queenofclean)

This cleaning method is also recommended by Ato Energy, which shares on its blog how much salt to use. After removing the standing water from your sink, it says, “Pour about half a cup of table salt down the drain before pouring in the hot water. Let it sit for a few minutes, and then flush with hot water to clear the mixture.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This flexible tool is designed to unclog drains by reaching 18 inches inside your drain. Once inserted, it can spin 360° to wrap around hair and other gunk before being removed. The set includes 5 disposable wand sticks for easy use, which can be attached to the removable handle.

For general maintenance and to keep your kitchen drain smelling fresh and free-flowing, Ato Energy suggests using vinegar and baking soda.

It suggests removing any standing water before pouring about a cup of baking soda into the drain. Then, follow with an equal amount of white or apple cider vinegar.

“The solution will bubble. That’s good! It means the chemical reaction is working,” it says.

Then, once the bubbles subside, it says to place a stopper on the drain and wait 15 minutes. You can then finish by running hot water down the drain to see if the clog has cleared. If there’s still a blockage, it advises repeating the above steps.

To avoid future blockages, ATCO Energy advises, “You can avoid tough clogs by watching what you pour down your sink. Never put bacon grease, coffee grounds or oils down your kitchen drain.”

#3398. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.
